summary.text: 面 began as a picture of a face: an enclosing outline surrounds an eye. Today it commonly means ‘face’; it is also used for ‘surface’ and ‘side’. In simplified Chinese, 面 also writes the flour and noodle word otherwise written 麵, a separate word history.

formation.text: Pictographic. The reported oracle graph depicts a face as an enclosing outline with an eye inside. The Shuowen account likewise describes the graph as shaped like a human face, derived from 𦣻; this is a historical explanation, while the oracle reading is a modern paleographic analysis. Neither a dated earliest inscription nor a bronze form of 面 itself is established here.

components.text: 面 is best described as one whole pictorial graph: the enclosing outline and eye together depict a face. Although the Shuowen account relates it to 𦣻, the supplied evidence does not establish that as a distinct current component, so the graph is not split into component records.

history.text: The oracle form is reported as an outline enclosing an eye; 面 itself is reported unattested in bronze inscriptions. A Chu-slip form is said to have an enclosure altered toward 臼. These reports describe written forms, not a fully documented sequence, and the cited artifacts were not independently inspected here.
The Shuowen explanation derives 面 from 𦣻 and describes it as shaped like a human face. 靣 is recorded as a variant, without evidence that it is an ancestor of 面.

The simplified character 面 is also used for the flour and noodle word written 麵 in traditional Chinese. The related graph 麪 is recorded as an older spelling analyzed with 麥 for meaning and 丏 for sound; evidence here does not establish the precise transition to 麵 or show that the face word 面 supplied the food word itself.

uncertainties.text: The earliest individual oracle inscriptions and their dates were not verified; the face interpretation is a reported modern analysis. The database reports no bronze form of 面, but the coverage limits behind that report are not known here.

The graph’s uses for ‘face toward’, ‘surface’, ‘side’ and ‘dimension’ are documented in dictionary or paleographic accounts, but their chronology and semantic links are not established by this evidence.

Evidence supports 麪 for flour or powder and later 麵 spelling, but does not establish the earliest separate attestations of flour and noodle senses, the exact graphic transition, or a borrowing of the face word based on sound.

senses.period: oracle-bone script period; individual attestations undated
senses.text: The oracle graph is interpreted as depicting a face, and the Shuowen gloss identifies the area before the face. Individual earliest inscriptions were not inspected or dated, so this is the earliest supported sense in the dossier, not a claim about the word’s absolute first use.

senses.period: Chu-slip text cited by a modern database; date not supplied
senses.text: 面 is reported in a Chu-slip text with the sense ‘face toward’.
Dictionary records include ‘surface’, ‘side’ and ‘dimension’. Their dates and relationships to the face and facing senses are not established here.

senses.gloss: flour, dough, noodles (written 面 in simplified Chinese for 麵)
senses.text: In simplified Chinese, 面 is used to write the flour and noodle word for which traditional Chinese uses 麵. This is a character-to-character writing substitution; the evidence does not show that the face meaning developed into the food meaning or establish a sound-based borrowing mechanism.

developments.text: The facing use is compatible with extension from the face sense, but the supplied evidence reports the use without establishing its historical path.

limitations.text: The dates of the facing, surface, side and dimension senses, and any links among them, remain unresolved in this evidence.
The food-word spelling relationship is supported, but neither its exact chronology nor a phonetic borrowing from the face word is established.

overview.text: 面 is a picture of a face, with an eye enclosed by an outline. It commonly means ‘face’; simplified Chinese also uses it to write the separate flour and noodle word otherwise written 麵.

components.text: Read the outline and eye together as one picture of a face; the evidence does not support splitting them into modern components.

relationships.text: In simplified Chinese, 面 is the standardized counterpart used for the traditional graph 麵 in the flour and noodle word. This whole-character relationship does not make 麵 an internal component of 面, and the evidence does not establish the exact date or a sound-based borrowing from the face word.
